name: Mandibular advancement surgery (BSSO)

card.summary: Established orthognathic operation that splits and moves the lower jaw forward; well studied for bite and function, and used by looksmaxxers to improve profile.
card.aka: BSSO, bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, sagittal split osteotomy
card.note: Major jaw surgery with a recognized risk of lasting numbness, relapse and joint changes; most research concerns functional rather than purely cosmetic outcomes.

quick.overview:
Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) is the standard operation for moving the lower jaw. The surgeon splits the jawbone lengthwise on each side behind the teeth, slides the tooth-bearing part forward and fixes it with plates and screws. It is used for recessed lower jaws, bite problems and some airway conditions, and is usually planned with an orthodontist.

In looksmaxxing communities it is a prominent hardmaxxing procedure, discussed alongside genioplasty, Le Fort upper-jaw surgery and implants as a way to improve the facial profile. Clinical research on BSSO is extensive, although most of it measures stability, nerve function and joint health rather than attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Cuts are made through the mouth along the inner and outer cortex of the lower jaw, allowing the front segment to be advanced. Titanium plates or screws hold the new position while the bone heals, which the Wikipedia article on orthognathic surgery says takes several weeks with fuller remodeling over a few months.
quick.risks: Documented risks include numbness of the lower lip and chin from inferior alveolar nerve injury, relapse of the advancement, changes in the jaw joint including condylar resorption, swelling, infection, and a liquid-diet recovery period. Studies report that neurosensory disturbance can persist in a share of patients.

lead: Mandibular advancement by bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) is an orthognathic operation in which the lower jaw is cut along the ramus on each side, split, and the tooth-bearing segment is moved forward and fixed in the new position. It is the most commonly described procedure for repositioning the mandible and is usually combined with orthodontic treatment.[1][2]

The operation is used medically for recessed lower jaws, bite problems, temporomandibular joint pathology and airway issues, and has a long clinical literature. Hugo Obwegeser is credited in the Wikipedia article on orthognathic surgery with developing the BSSO.[1] In looksmaxxing communities, BSSO is discussed as a way to improve profile and jawline, often with genioplasty and with Le Fort I upper-jaw surgery in so-called bimax surgery.[3][4]

Research on BSSO advancement addresses stability of the result, neurosensory disturbance, condylar remodeling and joint health, and patient well-being; the studies reviewed here are about function and surgical outcomes rather than perceived attractiveness.[5][6][7][8]
infobox: Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the mandible

paras: BSSO is a form of orthognathic surgery, which the Wikipedia article describes as surgery to reposition the jaws to treat skeletal and bite problems, sleep apnea and airway issues, TMJ disorders and facial asymmetry or proportion concerns, generally operating through the mouth with an orthodontist.[1] In BSSO, the mandible is cut on each side of the ramus and split so it can be moved forward or backward, then held with titanium plates or screws; older techniques wired the jaw shut for four to five weeks, which the article says is generally not done in modern practice.[1]

Forum discussions often distinguish BSSO from sliding genioplasty, which moves the chin only. One poster described a surgeon recommending genioplasty alone for a mildly recessed mandible, while other members argued that a narrow, weak jawline would need the jaw itself moved.[3] Others ask whether an aggressive genioplasty can mimic a BSSO, or in what order to combine BSSO, orthodontics and other procedures.[9][10]

The Wikipedia article places early published jaw surgery cases in 1849 and describes mandible and maxilla osteotomies from the 1940s, with Hugo Obwegeser developing the BSSO and the technique spreading from Germany to wider use.[1]

According to Wikipedia, initial healing takes two to six weeks, with full bone union and remodeling taking a further two to four months, and patients typically follow a liquid diet and often lose weight. Return to work is possible at two to six weeks.[1]

A 2009 systematic review of 24 studies examined horizontal relapse after BSSO advancement with rigid internal fixation, concluding on the causes and fixation types that influence it.[5] A prospective multicenter study with two-year follow-up of miniplate fixation analyzed condylar remodeling and resorption in relation to relapse.[11] A 2015 study used three-dimensional analysis of condylar remodeling and skeletal relapse after advancement.[12]

Numbness from injury to the inferior alveolar nerve is a recognized outcome. A study of 30 patients followed for a year examined subjective neurosensory disturbance in relation to age, magnitude of movement and nerve manipulation,[6] and a long-term study of 85 patients more than two years after surgery examined persistent neurosensory and functional sensory deficit by age group.[13] Wikipedia describes nerve numbness as usually temporary and typically recovering within three months, though rarely permanent.[1] A clinical and electrophysiologic evaluation of nerve injury diagnosis after sagittal split osteotomy has also been published.[14]

Studies of condylar resorption after bicortical screw fixation of advancement and of factors affecting condylar position address changes at the jaw joint.[15][16] A systematic review and meta-analysis asked whether orthognathic surgery causes or cures temporomandibular disorders.[7] Another study examined patients' functional and psychosocial well-being after surgical-orthodontic treatment.[8]

Human studies of BSSO advancement are numerous. They include a 2009 systematic review of relapse after advancement with rigid fixation,[5] prospective and retrospective series on neurosensory disturbance in groups of 30 and 85 patients,[6][13] a prospective multicenter study of miniplate stabilization with two-year follow-up,[11] studies of condylar resorption,[15] a systematic review and meta-analysis of orthognathic surgery and temporomandibular disorders,[7] and research on functional and psychosocial well-being after surgical-orthodontic treatment.[8] Most of these evaluate stability, nerve function and joint health rather than appearance specifically.

BSSO appears frequently in hardmaxxing threads on looksmax.org. Members post before-and-after photos, with one poster noting a crescent-shaped ramus from swelling three weeks after surgery, and others discuss combined procedures with genioplasty and Le Fort surgery, wisdom-tooth preservation planning and the cost of bimax surgery.[3][17][18][19] Some threads ask how to afford the procedure or where to find it at a lower price.[20][21]

timeline.event: Early published jaw surgery case reported by Simon Hullihen.[1]
Study of factors affecting neurosensory disturbance after BSSO published.[6]
Systematic review of stability after BSSO advancement with rigid fixation.[5]
Systematic review and meta-analysis on orthognathic surgery and temporomandibular disorders.[7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, BSSO is discussed as a major hardmaxxing option for a recessed jaw, often compared with genioplasty or paired with other jaw surgery.[3][17]

claims.claim: BSSO is a bigger improvement than genioplasty alone for a recessed lower third
claims.believers: Forum members argue that a genioplasty only lengthens or advances the chin, while BSSO moves the whole jaw forward and can fix a weak jawline.[3]
claims.experts: The surgeon in the same thread recommended genioplasty alone because it is less invasive, and Wikipedia describes the two as distinct procedures with different scopes.[1][3]

claims.claim: An aggressive genioplasty can mimic a BSSO
claims.believers: Users ask whether a large chin advancement can substitute for moving the jaw.[9]
claims.experts: No studies comparing the two for appearance were found among the sources reviewed.

claims.claim: BSSO carries a real risk of lasting numbness and relapse
claims.believers: Posters planning surgery discuss nerve, bone-cut placement and relapse as considerations.[6][18]
claims.experts: Published studies document neurosensory disturbance, horizontal relapse and condylar resorption after BSSO advancement.[5][6][13][15]
